extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, importers, distributors, SDS preparers, employers, and regulators (OSHA HCS stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for how manufacturers, importers, and distributors must classify and communicate chemical hazards under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS), including scope, intrinsic-hazard definition, SDS content, and limits based on knowledge/feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard classification scope (intrinsic properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazard classification shall include any hazards associated with the chemical's intrinsic properties including: (i) a change in the chemical's physical form and; (ii) chemical reaction products associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the regulatory text finalized by OSHA to tie classification obligations to intrinsic properties; it explicitly lists two examples (change in physical form; chemical reaction products from known/reasonably anticipated uses). OSHA framed this as a clarification (not a substantive expansion) and added the term 'intrinsic' to make clear the basis for classification. See discussion justifying inclusion (preamble) and references to prior guidance and LOIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include classified hazards in SDS Section 2
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazards identified and classified under both paragraphs (d)(1)(i) and (d)(1)(ii) must be included in Section 2 of the product's SDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies that Section 2 of the Safety Data Sheet is specifically required to contain hazard information on hazards resulting from a change in physical form and from chemical reaction products when those hazards are known or reasonably anticipated. While related information may appear elsewhere in the SDS, Section 2 is the place for presenting hazard classifications for quick access by workers and emergency responders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling exclusion for certain reaction-product hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is changing the language in paragraph (f)(1) to clarify that hazards identified and classified under new paragraph (d)(1)(ii) will not be required to appear on a product's label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such hazards must be classified and included in the SDS (Section 2), OSHA clarified that chemical reaction products associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses are not necessarily required to be placed on the immediate product label. See Summary and Explanation of paragraph (f)(1) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification tied to what is known or reasonably anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule ties a responsible party's classification obligations to what the manufacturer, importer, or distributor knows or can reasonably anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA does not require prediction of every conceivable downstream use; classification is limited to hazards arising from uses that are known or that a knowledgeable person could reasonably anticipate. The agency cites prior LOIs, guidance, and examples (e.g., aerosol degreasers, hair-straightening products/formaldehyde) to illustrate what would be reasonably anticipated in particular industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable effort to obtain reliable downstream-use information
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturer's or importer's hazard classification must anticipate the full range of downstream uses of its products and account for any hazardous by-products that are known to be present and may be formed; manufacturers 'must make a reasonable effort to obtain reliable information' to determine how their product(s) or by-product(s) may expose workers under normal conditions of use or in foreseeable emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explained manufacturers are not required to contact every downstream workplace, but should use product stewardship programs, industry knowledge, and other reasonable means to obtain relevant information. LOIs and prior guidance (2015, 2016) provide context for what constitutes a reasonable effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification based on intrinsic/inherent hazards (not exposure level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazard classification is based on the intrinsic or inherent properties of the chemical that are presented in the workplace and are not tied to the level of exposure to the chemical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA distinguishes intrinsic hazards from non-intrinsic effects (examples: scalds from high temperature or slips from spilled liquids are not intrinsic). Intrinsic hazards are derived from the essential nature of the substance, reaction product, or mixture. Changes in physical form and reaction products are considered intrinsic where the property would not be true of any substance simply under those conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement when downstream use is proprietary/CBI
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA would not consider a manufacturer or supplier to know or be able to reasonably anticipate a downstream use if the downstream user uses the chemical in a proprietary process producing derivatives that are trade secrets; therefore this situation would not trigger classification requirements under paragraph (d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a carve-out: if downstream uses are withheld for confidential business information reasons, the upstream party is not held to knowledge/anticipation standard for those uses. The preamble affirms that lack of downstream information due to trade secrets relieves the upstream party from classifying those unknown downstream hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No expectation to classify every use for multi-use feedstocks/commodity chemicals
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA would not expect manufacturers of feedstocks, starting materials, commodity chemicals, solvents, reactants, or chemical intermediates, which could have thousands of uses, to classify hazards of downstream products that use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such chemicals with extremely broad or innumerable downstream uses (e.g., toluene), manufacturers should ensure appropriate information appears in Section 10 (stability and reactivity) of the SDS to help downstream manufacturers assess specific process risks. OSHA recognizes practical limits and does not require exhaustive downstream classification in these circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith effort standard and feasibility/economic consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must make a good faith effort to provide downstream users with sufficient information about hazards associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses; OSHA determined based on the record that the requirements of the final rule are economically feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA reviewed stakeholder concerns about feasibility and burdens, acknowledged limits, and concluded the clarified obligations are feasible. Product stewardship programs, industry engagement, surveys, and other practices cited by commenters are examples of how to meet the good faith/feasibility expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicative classification; responsibility for one's own product
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers of chemicals are responsible for the classification of their own chemical products; upstream parties are not required to independently and duplicatively classify downstream products unless they know or could reasonably anticipate the downstream uses with sufficient information to classify the hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA rejected concerns that the clarification would force all upstream suppliers to redundantly classify downstream products. The requirement is limited to situations where the upstream party has or should have sufficient knowledge about the downstream use; downstream users remain responsible for classifying hazards specific to their processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meaning of 'reasonably anticipated' (precedent and factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'reasonably anticipated' ties classification scope to what a knowledgeable person would expect to occur based on factors such as nature of precursors, type of reaction, manufacturing process, products produced, intended uses, or associated use conditions (illustrated by EPA TSCA and other agency uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes that 'reasonably anticipated' is used in other standards and guidance (bloodborne pathogens, silica, HAZWOPER, NTP listings, TSCA examples) and points to factors that can inform whether a use is reasonably anticipated. This helps practitioners apply the standard consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of related information elsewhere in the SDS does not replace Section 2 requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Although similar information may be contained in multiple SDS sections and used for different purposes, the changes to paragraph (d)(1) specifically require Section 2 to contain information on hazards resulting from a change in the chemical's physical form and from chemical reaction products when they are known or can be reasonably anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explains the standardized SDS format improves accessibility: immediate hazard information should be presented early (Section 2) for employees and emergency responders, while more technical detail appears later. Stakeholder claims that other sections already cover the information do not negate the Section 2 requirement.
